'''brimfulness''' (brim′fu̇l′nes), ''n.'' The state of being brimful; fullness to the top. [Rare.]

'''brimless''' (brim′les), ''a.'' [< ''brim''<sup>2</sup> + ''-less''.] Having no brim: as, a ''brimless'' hat.

'''brimly†''', ''adv.'' [Early mod. E. also ''breemly'', ''bremely'', < ME. ''brymly'', ''bremly'', ''bremely''; < ''brim''<sup>4</sup> + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.] '''1.''' Violently; fiercely; terribly.
{{smaller block|<poem>The kynge blyschit [looked] one the beryne with his brode eghne [eyes]
That fulle ''brymly'' for breth brynte as the gledys.</poem>
{{right|''Morte Arthure'', l. 116.}}}}
'''2.''' Hastily; quickly.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Brymly'' before us be thai broght,
Our dedes that shalle dam us bidene.</poem>
{{right|''Towneley Mysteries'', p. 105.}}}}
'''3.''' Loudly.
{{smaller block|<poem>Briddes ful ''bremely'' on the bowes singe.</poem>
{{right|''William of Palerne'', l. 23.}}
<poem>Thou hast blown thy blast ''breemlye'' abroad.</poem>
{{right|''Percy Fol. MS.'', iii. 71.}}}}

'''brimme<sup>1</sup>†''', '''brimme<sup>2</sup>†'''. See ''brim''<sup>1</sup>, ''brim''<sup>2</sup>, etc.

'''brimmed''' (brimd), ''p. a.'' [< ''brim''<sup>2</sup> + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.] '''1.''' Having a brim; in composition, having a brim of the kind specified: as, a broad-''brimmed'' hat. —'''2.''' Filled to the brim; level with the brim.
{{smaller block|<poem>May thy ''brimmed'' waves for this
Their full tribute never miss.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', Comus, l. 924.}}}}

'''brimmer''' (brim′ėr), ''n.'' [< ''brim''<sup>2</sup>, ''n.'', + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' A bowl full to the top.

'''brimstony''' (brim′stō-ni), ''a.'' [< ''brimstone'' + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.] Full of or containing brimstone; resembling brimstone; sulphurous: as, “''brimstony'', blue, and fiery,” ''B. Jonson'', Alchemist, iv. 5. [Rare.]

'''brin'''<sup>1</sup>†, ''v.'' An obsolete variant of ''burn''<sup>1</sup>. ''Chaucer.''

'''brin'''<sup>2</sup> (brin), ''n.'' [F., a blade, shoot; origin unknown.] One of the radiating sticks of a fan.

'''brinch'''† (brinch), ''v. i.'' [Also written ''brince'', early mod. E. ''brynch'', also ''brindice'', < It. ''brindisi'', ''brindesi'' (Florio), F. ''brinde'', formerly ''bringue'' (Cotgrave), a drinking to, a toast.] To drink in answer to a pledge; pledge one in drinking.

'''brinded''' (brin′ded), ''a.'' [Same as E. dial. and Sc. ''branded'', of a reddish-brown color with streaks or patches of darker brown or black (> ''brandie'', a name often given to cows in Scot-

land); the vowel modified, appar. after Icel. ''brönd-'' in deriv. ''bröndōttr'', brinded, as a cow, for *''brandōttr'' (cf. ''brand-krossōttr'', brinded with a white cross on the forehead), < ''brandr'' = E. ''brand''. Thus ''brinded'', as above, is nearly equiv. to ''branded'', pp. of ''brand'', ''v.'': see ''brand''.] '''1.''' Properly, of a gray or tawny color marked with bars or streaks of a darker hue; brindled: applied more loosely to any animal having a hide variegated by streaks or spots, and by Milton to the lioness, whose hide is of a nearly uniform hue: as, “the ''brinded'' cat,” ''Shak.'', Macbeth, iv. 1; “three ''brinded'' cows,” ''Dryden'', Cock and Fox.
{{smaller block|<poem>She tamed the ''brinded'' lioness
And spotted mountain-pard.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', Comus, l. 443.}}
<poem>The ''brinded'' catamount, that lies
High in the boughs to watch his prey.</poem>
{{right|''Bryant'', Hunter of the Prairies.}}}}
'''2.''' In ''her.'', spotted: said of a beast used as a bearing.

'''brindle''' (brin′dl), ''n.'' [Assumed from ''brindled''.] '''1.''' The state of being brinded; a color or mixture of colors, of which gray is the base, with bands of a darker gray or black color: as, “a natural ''brindle'',” ''Richardson'', Clarissa Harlowe. —'''2.''' A name of the mudfish or bowfin, ''Amia calva''. See cut under ''Amiidæ''.

'''brindled''' (brin′dld), ''a.'' [A kind of dim. form of ''brinded''.] Brinded; variegated with streaks of different colors.
{{smaller block|<poem>And there the wild-cat’s ''brindled'' hide
The frontlet of the elk adorns.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', L. of the L., i. 27.}}}}

'''brine<sup>1</sup>''' (brīn), ''n.'' [= Sc. (irreg.) ''brime'', < ME. ''brine'', ''bryne'', < AS. ''bryne'' (= MD. ''brijn''), brine, salt liquor; a particular use of ''bryne'' (early ME. {{right|''Donne'', Love’s Diet.}}}}

'''brine<sup>2</sup>†''', ''n.'' [Cf. North. E. ''brim'', the forehead; < ME. ''bryne'', brow, < Icel. ''brūn'', pl. ''brȳnn'', mod. ''brȳr'', brow, = Sw. Dan. ''bryn'', brow: see ''brow''.] The eyebrow.

{{right|''Prompt. Parv.'', p. 51.}}}}

{{smaller block|<poem>She from a carved press ''brought'' him linen fair,
And a new-woven coat a king might wear.</poem>{{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, I. 295.}}}}
'''2.''' To cause to come or accrue; be the means of conveying possession of; impart; devolve upon: as, the transaction ''brought'' great profit; his wife ''brought'' him a large dowry.
{{smaller block|<poem>She shall ''bring'' him [in marriage] that
Which he not dreams of.</poem>{{right|''Shak.'', W. T., iv. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Music that ''brings'' sweet sleep.</poem>{{right|''Tennyson'', Choric Song, i.}}}}
'''3.''' To cause to come or pass, as to a new place, state, or condition; impel; draw on; lead: as, to ''bring'' one to a better mind.
{{smaller block|The fortress . . . shall he ''bring'' . . . to the ground. {{right|Isa. xxv. 12.}}}}
{{smaller block|God had ''brought'' their counsels to naught. Neh. iv. 15.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>We ''bring'' to one dead level ev’ry mind.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Dunciad, iv. 268.}}}}
{{smaller block|Profitable employments would be a diversion, if men could but be ''brought'' to delight in them.
{{right|''Locke.''}}}}
'''4.''' To aid in coming or passing, as to one’s home or destination; conduct; attend; accompany.
{{smaller block|<poem>Yet give leave, my lord,
That we may ''bring'' you something on the way.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., i. 1.}}}}
'''5.''' To convey or put forth as a product; bear or be the bearer of; yield: as, the land ''brings'' good harvests.
{{smaller block|<poem>Because she ''brought'' him none but girls, she thought
Her husband loved her not. ''B. Jonson'', New Inn, i. 1.</poem>}}
'''6.''' To convey to the mind or knowledge; make known on coming, or coming before one; bear or impart a declaration of.
{{smaller block|Be thou there until I ''bring'' thee word. Mat. iii. 13.}}
{{smaller block|What accusation ''bring'' ye against this man?
{{right|John xviii. 29.}}}}
'''7.''' To fetch or put forward before a tribunal; make a presentation of; institute; declare in or as if in court: as, to ''bring'' an action or an indictment against one; the jury ''brought'' the prisoner in guilty.
{{smaller block|<poem>I’ll ''bring'' mine action on the proudest he
That stops my way. ''Shak.'', T. of the S., iii. 2.</poem>}}
{{smaller block|A friend of mine here was doubting whether he should ''bring'' an action against two persons on so unfortunate a day as Saturday.
{{right|''E. W. Lane'', Modern Egyptians, I. 340.}}}}

'''8.''' To cause to become; make to be.
{{smaller block|I was ''brought'' acquainted with a Burgundian Jew who had married an apostate Kentish woman.
{{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, Aug. 28, 1641.}}}}

'''To bring about''', to effect; accomplish.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
